tagline.text: The site of the 1944 landing, a town of liberation with Hill 120

location.label: Location
location.text: Eastern coast of Leyte Island, a town on Leyte Gulf (about 36 km south of Tacloban)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,200 (per person, based on a round-trip day trip from Tacloban including transport and meals)

children.text: Dulag is a coastal town facing Leyte Gulf, called the "Liberation Town" because American forces landed here in October 1944. From Tacloban you can visit the 120 steps of Hill 120, where the first American flag is said to have been raised, the memorials and Our Lady of Refuge Church in half a day.

Dulag is a second-class municipality on the eastern coast of Leyte Island facing Leyte Gulf. According to Wikipedia, Tolosa to the north is about 12 km away, Julita to the west about 7 km and Mayorga to the south about 7 km, and it is about 36 km south of Tacloban, around an hour along the Maharlika Highway. Its area is 110.70 square kilometers, its 2024 population is 50,728 and it has 45 barangays (11 urban and 34 rural). About 97.75 percent of the population speaks Waray and about 97.21 percent is Roman Catholic. The highest point is 889 m and the town center is at 19 m. It was once a trading center where abaca, copra, tobacco, rice and wine were exchanged, and today farming and fishing villages continue along the low coastal plain. The population grew steadily from 14,884 in 1903, 31,185 in 1948, 38,897 in 2000 and 47,300 in 2015, and poverty incidence fell from 45.57 percent in 2000 to 27.02 percent in 2023. In 2024 the municipality's revenue was about ₱275 million and its assets about ₱782.7 million. It is a small town with few tourist facilities, so it is best seen as a trip to look at historic sites.

The most important moment in Dulag's history was October 1944. American forces landed here from October 17 to 20, and naval shelling destroyed the church, public buildings and homes. The seat of government was temporarily moved to Mayorga, and Mayor Marcial Lagunzad was killed in an American bombing raid in the early days of liberation. Mayor Nicolas Bautista then led the rebuilding. Some veterans claim that General Douglas MacArthur landed in Dulag before Palo, but Wikipedia presents this as a local claim rather than established fact. That is why the name "Liberation Town" is often used for Dulag. At about the same time, in Barangay Tanghas in neighboring Tolosa, Irving Berlin is recorded as having first performed "Heaven Watch the Philippines" for a Filipino audience.

The earlier history is also deep. The Jesuit missionaries Fr. Alonzo de Humanes and Fr. Juan del Campo arrived in September 1595 with the encomendero Don Pedro Hernandez, who brought them over from Cebu. Moro raiders struck on October 29, 1603 and again in 1613. The Jesuits built a brick church dedicated to the Nativity of Our Lady, called the "Refugio" (refuge), and after they left in 1768 the Augustinians took over the parish. The first Franciscan parish priest arrived in 1843 and is said to have directed the building of the first road to Abuyog. In 1954 Mayorga was separated from Dulag. The present Our Lady of Refuge Parish Church is presented as matching the church in veterans' accounts, and a Catholic directory gives the parish history as dating to 1661.

What to see in Dulag comes down to two things. One is Hill 120, where the historical marker says that at 10:42 a.m. on October 20, 1944, 1st Lt. Clifford W. Mills of the 3rd Battalion, 382nd Infantry, 96th Division raised the American flag. That was 42 minutes after the landing, and it is described as the first American flag raised on Philippine soil after the flag was lowered at Bataan on April 9, 1942. The marker faces the main highway of Dulag, and a concrete staircase leads to the top in about 5 minutes. At the top there are a Japanese memorial, a cenotaph honoring Filipino, Japanese and American dead, a marker for unknown American soldiers and the badges of the 96th Division, the "Deadeyes." The other is the church and the town streets, and travel site listings also include a Japanese Tunnel, though little information is available on its location and opening.

blocks.title: Hill 120 World War II memorial site

children.text: A hill where the historical marker says the first American flag was raised on Philippine soil on October 20, 1944. A concrete staircase takes about 5 minutes to climb, and at the top are a Japanese memorial, a cenotaph for Filipino, Japanese and American dead, a marker for unknown American soldiers and the 96th Division badge. The view at the top is blocked by many coconut palms.

blocks.title: Our Lady of Refuge Parish Church

children.text: A parish that continues from the Nativity of Our Lady brick church "Refugio," built by the Jesuits in 1595. The church is recorded as having been shattered by shelling during the 1944 landing. Avoid Mass times and visit quietly.
Some veterans say General MacArthur landed first in Dulag. Wikipedia presents this as a local claim. Do not take it as established fact, and compare local markers and museum materials.
A World War II relic listed on travel sites. Little information is available on its location and whether it is open. Ask the municipal tourism office or locals first.

blocks.title: MacArthur Leyte Landing Memorial in Palo (nearby)

children.text: The memorial park known for MacArthur's landing is not in Dulag but in Barangay Candahug in Palo, about 5 km south of Tacloban, on about 6.78 hectares. A reviewer says parking is free and you should not expect restaurants or restrooms. Early morning or late afternoon is best. Seeing it with Dulag lets you follow the same landing story at two places.

A low coast where Leyte Gulf can be seen from town. It is a good place to look at the sea where the landing took place and reflect on history. Information on swimming and other activities could not be confirmed.

Barangay Tanghas in Tolosa, about 12 km north of Dulag, is recorded as the place where Irving Berlin first performed "Heaven Watch the Philippines." It is a good place to continue the history of the landing period together with Dulag.
Take a jeepney or van to Dulag from the Tacloban transport terminal. It takes about 1 hour.
Arrive in Dulag and climb the steps of Hill 120 in front of the marker by the main road.
Look around the memorials and cenotaphs at the top.
Walk around Our Lady of Refuge Church and the town streets.
Have lunch in town.
Return to Tacloban, where you can also continue to the Leyte Landing Memorial in Palo.
Check the time of the last transport back in advance.

items.title: Landing sites route
items.subtitle: Palo and Dulag in one day

children.text: From Tacloban, go first to the Leyte Landing Memorial in Candahug, Palo, and walk around the quiet park in the early morning.
Return to the Tacloban transport terminal and take a jeepney to Dulag.
Climb the steps of Hill 120 in Dulag and look around the markers.
Have lunch in town.
See Our Lady of Refuge Church and return to Tacloban.
The two sites tell the same landing story but are some distance apart, so allow plenty of travel time.
Fly from Manila to Tacloban (TAC). Check flight schedules on the airline's website.
From the airport to the city transport terminal, take a jeepney or taxi.

Jeepneys to Dulag leave from the Tacloban transport terminal. A 2009 post says it takes about 1 hour, and Wikipedia says it is about 36 km from Tacloban, 45 minutes to 1 hour along the Maharlika Highway.
Check the fare locally.
Jeepney routes change over time. Check at the terminal.
Get around town by tricycle. Agree on the fare before you ride.
Hill 120 is by the main road, so you can get off and walk.

Dulag is comfortable for walking and climbing steps in the dry season from December to May. Around the anniversary of the landing, October 17–20, there may be local events, so check with the municipal office.

According to modeled climate data, annual rainfall is about 1,598 mm, with about 269 rainy days a year. Average daily highs are 28–30°C and lows are 22–25°C. The text and the monthly table in Wikipedia disagree on the rainiest month, so check the latest weather before you go.

There is almost no information on lodging in Dulag town, so most travelers stay in Tacloban and make a round trip in a day. Information on restaurants in town could not be confirmed. The safe plan is to find lunch locally or have it after returning to Tacloban.

The town has a municipal health office, and electricity is supplied by the DORELCO cooperative. Piped water reaches only some households, and many homes use pump wells. For education there is the Dulag satellite campus of Eastern Visayas State University. The postal code is 6505 and the area code is 053.
Hill 120 is said to have 120 steps. Climb in the morning to avoid the midday sun.
The view at the top is blocked by coconut palms. Go to read the markers and see the memorials rather than for the view.
If you are connecting with a Tacloban trip, seeing the Leyte Landing Memorial in Palo together makes the landing story easier to understand.
The claim that MacArthur landed first is a local one. Compare the markers and museum materials.
Check the time of the last transport back on the way in.
Bring water and a hat. There may be little shade on the steps at the top, and reading the markers and taking photos as you climb slowly helps you understand the meaning of the memorials better.
This is a town with little information available. Check opening hours and entry rules locally and leave some slack in your schedule.
Low-lying barangays can flood during typhoons. Keep your plans flexible in the rainy season.
Keep quiet at the memorials and cenotaphs, and do not climb on the monuments.
